North Carolina counties assess and collect property tax, and owners can appeal to the county board of equalization and review.

What the official sources say

  • County board of equalization and review is composed of the county commissioners unless a special board is appointed. (N.C.G.S. 105-322(a); source)
  • The board holds its first meeting not earlier than the first Monday in April and not later than the first Monday in May. (N.C.G.S. 105-322(e); source)
  • In a revaluation year the board must finish by December 1. (N.C.G.S. 105-322(e); source)
  • A taxpayer's hearing request must be made in writing or by personal appearance before the board adjourns. (N.C.G.S. 105-322(g)(2)a; source)
  • The board must notify the appellant by mail of its action within 30 days after adjournment. (N.C.G.S. 105-322(g)(2)d; source)
  • Counties must reappraise all real property at least every eighth year; counties of 75,000+ must advance reappraisal if sales assessment ratio is below .85 or above 1.15. (N.C.G.S. 105-286; source)
  • Property tax lien attaches on the date property is to be listed (January 1, per 105-285 cross-reference). (N.C.G.S. 105-355(a); source)
  • Penalties, interest and costs attach at the same time as the tax lien. (N.C.G.S. 105-355(a); source)
  • Tax lien foreclosure by civil action in the nature of a mortgage foreclosure; owner of record, spouse and lienholders must be served. (N.C.G.S. 105-374(a),(c); source)

North Carolina offers a property tax exclusion for qualifying elderly or disabled homeowners.

What the official sources say

  • Income limit started at $25,000 for 2008 and is adjusted yearly by the Social Security COLA; NCDOR sets it each year. (N.C.G.S. 105-277.1(a2); source)
  • Application should be filed in the regular listing period but must be accepted through June 1 preceding the tax year. (N.C.G.S. 105-277.1(c); source)
  • Circuit breaker: owner 65+/disabled with 5 years' ownership and occupancy and income up to 150% of the limit may defer taxes above 4% (or 5%) of income. (N.C.G.S. 105-277.1B(d),(f); source)
  • Circuit breaker deferred taxes (prior 3 years) become due when the owner transfers the residence, dies (unless passing to co-owner/spouse who occupies), or stops using it as permanent residence. (N.C.G.S. 105-277.1B(h),(i); source)

What we could not confirm

  • The current income limit, which we did not confirm on an opened page.

North Carolina homestead exemption FAQ

Where do I apply for the homestead exclusion?

With the county tax office. Confirm the application window with your county.

What does the North Carolina homestead exclusion do?

It takes part of a qualifying owner's home value off the tax rolls. Under the elderly or disabled exclusion, the amount removed is whichever is bigger: a fixed $25,000, or one half of what the county appraises the residence at.

North Carolina runs three owner-relief programs, and one form covers them all. Form AV-9 goes to your county tax assessor, since the Department of Revenue does not take it. An owner can collect from just one program at a time, so the choice matters.

Who qualifies for the elderly or disabled exclusion in North Carolina?

You qualify when, on the January 1 before the tax year, you live in North Carolina, are at least 65 years old or has a total and permanent disability, and had prior-year income at or under the cap. The rule sits in Chapter 105, section 277.1 of the General Statutes.

  • NCDOR's 2026 form prints the income cap as $38,800, up from $37,900 for 2025. It tracks the Social Security cost-of-living percentage.
  • Income counts money from every source, with gifts or inheritances from a spouse, parent, grandparent or descendant left out. Spouses who share a home combine their incomes.
  • A protected residence is the dwelling plus its lot up to one acre and related improvements. Houses, apartments in multi-family buildings and manufactured homes all fit.
  • Disability must be certified by a physician licensed in this state or by a government agency.
  • A couple gets the whole exclusion even if only one spouse meets the test.

How is the disabled veteran exclusion different in North Carolina?

It takes $45,000 off the appraised figure, and NCDOR's own form says the program has no age or income limit. Its statute is section 277.1C.

The veteran must live in this state, hold an honorable or under-honorable-conditions discharge, and either draw benefits under 38 U.S.C. 2101 or hold a VA certification of permanent and total service-connected disability. An unmarried surviving spouse can claim it as well. Start with a Veterans Service Officer on Form NCDVA-9, then file that form at the assessor's office.

What is the North Carolina circuit breaker deferral?

It sets a ceiling on the tax bill as a slice of household income and postpones the rest. The ceiling is 4.0% of income for owners at or below the cap, and 5.0% for owners above the cap but within 150% of it.

NCDOR's 2026 form prints those two thresholds as $38,800 and $58,200. Applicants must be at least 65 or has a total and permanent disability, live in this state, and have spent five years owning and occupying the house as their permanent residence. Filing is yearly, not once.

The postponed tax becomes a lien. When a disqualifying event hits, whether a transfer, the owner's death or moving out, the deferred taxes of the previous three fiscal years come due.

How do the three North Carolina relief programs compare?

Source: sections 105-277.1, 105-277.1B and 105-277.1C, plus NCDOR's 2026 Form AV-9
ProgramWhat it doesWho it is forIncome test
Elderly or disabled exclusionCuts the bigger of $25,000 and half the appraisalAt least 65, or with a total and permanent disability$38,800 for 2026
Disabled veteran exclusionTakes $45,000 off the appraised figureQualifying disabled veteran or unmarried surviving spouseNone
Circuit breakerLimits tax to 4.0% or 5.0% of income and defers the excessAt least 65, or disabled, with five years in the homeUp to $58,200 for 2026

When and where do owners apply for North Carolina homestead relief?

Take Form AV-9 to the county tax assessor during the January listing window, which opens on the first working day of the year and closes January 31. A late application is still taken through the first of June.

One form serves all three programs, so pick the one that fits and ask the assessor whether you meet more than one test. The income cap resets every year, so use the form for the tax year you are claiming.

What papers should a North Carolina applicant bring to the assessor?

Ask the assessor's office for its checklist, because each county handles intake itself. The statutes point to the evidence most files need.

  • Proof of age, or the certificate of permanent and total disability.
  • Prior-year income records for the owner and for a spouse in the same home.
  • Proof the property is the owner's permanent residence, with acreage if the lot exceeds one acre.
  • For the circuit breaker, evidence of five years of ownership and occupancy.
  • For the veteran exclusion, the VA certification or benefits record and a completed Form NCDVA-9.

Bringing everything on the first visit saves a second trip and keeps you inside the January window.

How does the North Carolina income cap move from year to year?

NCDOR resets the number annually with the Social Security cost-of-living percentage. The 2026 form shows $38,800 against $37,900 for 2025, and its $58,200 upper circuit breaker line equals 150% of the 2026 cap.

An owner just over the line one year can land under it the next, so one denial does not decide later years. The circuit breaker requires a fresh application every year. Ask the assessor whether your county wants repeat filings for the other two programs.

Can an owner also appeal the appraised value in North Carolina?

Yes, and the appraisal matters because every program here is measured against it. The county commissioners normally sit as the review board, and its first meeting falls in spring, between early April and early May.

Ask for a hearing, in writing or in person, before the board adjourns. The board mails its decision within 30 days after adjournment, and an owner who disagrees may take the matter to the Property Tax Commission by written notice within 30 days after that mailing. Because the elderly or disabled version takes the bigger of a flat figure and half the value, a lower appraisal can change which side of that comparison controls. Call your assessor for the county's own appeal calendar and forms.

What happens to this relief when you sell a North Carolina home?

A sale is a transfer, and a transfer is one of the events that makes deferred circuit breaker tax payable. Ask the county tax collector for a written payoff before the closing date so the amount can be settled at the table.

  • The seller owes the county deed excise tax at the register's office ahead of filing the deed: one dollar per five hundred of price, counting any partial five hundred.
  • Each year's bill falls due September 1, and anything unpaid picks up 2% interest on January 6.
  • Heirs who inherit from a circuit breaker owner may meet the deferred bill too, because the owner's death is a triggering event.

Deferred tax is a lien, so clear it with the collector rather than leaving the buyer to find it. If you already receive any of the three benefits, mention that to your closing agent at the outset so the payoff request reaches the county early.

More questions about North Carolina Homestead Exclusion

How large is the North Carolina homestead exclusion?

The elderly or disabled version cuts the bigger of $25,000 and half the appraisal. The veteran version removes a flat $45,000.

What is the 2026 income limit for the North Carolina exclusion?

The 2026 NCDOR form prints $38,800. The same form lists $37,900 as the 2025 limit.

Where do I file the North Carolina homestead application?

With your county tax assessor on Form AV-9. Veterans first complete Form NCDVA-9 with a Veterans Service Officer.

Can I get more than one North Carolina homestead program?

No. The three programs are alternatives, and an owner draws on one of them.

What if I miss the January 31 filing date in North Carolina?

You still have time. Assessors must accept applications until June 1 of the tax year.

North Carolina evictions are called summary ejectment and run through the register of deeds and magistrates.

What the official sources say

  • Summary ejectment applies to a tenant holding over after term expires or after lease breach by which estate ceased. (N.C.G.S. 42-26(a); source)
  • Clerk issues summons requiring answer at a time not exceeding seven days from issuance (excluding weekends and holidays). (N.C.G.S. 42-28; source)
  • Magistrate gives judgment for possession if plaintiff proves case, defendant admits, or defendant fails to appear. (N.C.G.S. 42-30; source)
  • Unpaid water, sewer or electric charges cannot be the basis for lease termination. (N.C.G.S. 42-26(b); source)
  • Foreclosure notice of sale on residential property under 15 units must be mailed to occupants under a rental agreement (or 'occupant'). (N.C.G.S. 45-21.17(4); source)
  • NC courts refer to G.S. 45-21.33A for effect of foreclosure on a preexisting tenancy. (NC Judicial Branch: Foreclosures; source)
  • Tenants in possession under unrecorded leases are not 'record owners' for foreclosure notice. (N.C.G.S. 45-21.16(b)(3); source)
Selling in North Carolina?
We buy North Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What we could not confirm

  • Whether a voluntary sale ends a lease.

What is the eviction process in North Carolina called?

North Carolina calls it summary ejectment. The landlord files a complaint, the clerk of superior court issues a summons, and a magistrate in small claims court hears the case. Possession is enforced by the sheriff, not by the landlord.

The grounds are in G.S. 42-26: a tenant who holds over after the term, a tenant who breaches a lease condition that ends the estate, or a tenant who deserts the premises while in arrears. The process is built to be fast, and each step has a short deadline.

If you own a rented house and want to sell it, the steps below show how long a vacant house can take to deliver, and which steps you can skip by working out a move date with the tenant.

How does a North Carolina eviction case move from filing to possession?

It moves in five steps: notice, complaint, hearing, judgment and writ. The table puts each step beside the timing the statutes and the court system print.

StepWhat the sources say
SummonsClerk sets an appearance date no more than seven days after issuance, weekends and legal holidays excluded (G.S. 42-28)
HearingSmall claims dates are set within 30 days of filing, usually within 10 to 15 days for evictions (NC Judicial Branch)
Short serviceContinuance is mandatory if the defendant was served fewer than two days before court (NC Judicial Branch)
JudgmentMagistrate orders possession if the plaintiff proves the case, the defendant admits it, or the defendant does not appear (G.S. 42-30)
AppealNotice of appeal to district court within 10 days of the magistrate's decision (NC Judicial Branch)
WritSheriff must execute within five days of receiving the writ (G.S. 42-36.2)

Sources: G.S. 42-28, G.S. 42-30, G.S. 42-36.2 and the NC Judicial Branch small claims page.

What does it cost to file a summary ejectment case?

The court prints a small claims filing fee of $96 and a sheriff service fee of $30. There is no jury trial in small claims, which keeps the hearing short. These court figures are as printed on the Judicial Branch page, so confirm them with the clerk before you file.

The landlord can also claim rent in arrears and damages for occupation after the lease ended, up to the small claims limit in G.S. 7A-210(1). The summons statute says a landlord who leaves those claims out does not lose them in another action.

G.S. 42-46 controls what a landlord can add to the bill. It lets a landlord recover court filing fees, service costs and reasonable attorney fees under a written lease, with a cap of fifteen percent of the amount owed. It also permits one administrative fee per case, and only if the lease allows it.

  • A complaint-filing fee, if the tenant cures and the landlord dismisses before judgment.
  • A court-appearance fee of ten percent of the monthly rent, if the landlord wins in small claims.
  • A second-trial fee of up to twelve percent of the monthly rent after a tenant's appeal.

What can a tenant do after the magistrate rules?

A tenant who loses can give notice of appeal to district court, orally in court or in writing within 10 days of the magistrate's decision. The Judicial Branch notes that appeal costs must be paid and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

That bond matters to a landlord who is also a seller. If the tenant appeals and posts what the court requires, the writ can be held up and a buyer may have to wait. A landlord can plan around that by asking the buyer for a closing date that leaves room for the appeal window.

If the tenant does not appeal, the landlord asks for the writ. Before removing belongings, the sheriff gives notice of the approximate time. That notice is delivered to the tenant or left at the home at least two days before the stated time, or mailed first class at least five days before.

What happens to the tenant's belongings after a writ?

Within seven days after the landlord is placed in lawful possession, the tenant may ask for property back, and the landlord must release it during regular business hours or at an agreed time. During that period a landlord may move items for storage but may not throw away or sell them, under G.S. 42-36.2.

After seven days, if the landlord offered to release the property and the tenant did not retrieve it, the landlord may dispose of it as G.S. 42-25.9(g) allows. If the sheriff stores the property, the sheriff can require the landlord to advance the cost of delivery and one month of storage.

  • Do not clear out belongings before the writ is executed.
  • Offer release in writing and keep a copy.
  • Photograph the house when you receive possession.

These steps affect a sale because a buyer who wants the house empty will ask when the house is clear and how the contents were handled.

Can I sell a rented house in North Carolina while an eviction is pending?

A pending case changes what you can promise a buyer, because the delivery date depends on the hearing, any appeal and the sheriff. Ask your attorney how the contract should treat the case and who keeps the claim for back rent.

If the house is headed for foreclosure instead, the tenant's position differs. Under G.S. 45-21.16A, the notice of sale for a residential property with fewer than 15 rental units must say an order for possession may issue. A tenant under a rental agreement entered or renewed on or after October 1, 2007 may end the lease on at least 10 and no more than 90 days' notice after the sale date.

In a foreclosure the hearing takes place before the clerk of superior court, and notice of the hearing must be served at least 10 days ahead. A tenant who gets a foreclosure notice should read it closely and ask an attorney about the dates.

What should a North Carolina landlord do first?

Match the tenancy to the right notice and ground, gather the lease and payment records, and file with the clerk in the county where the house is. Then ask for the hearing date and plan the sale around it.

  • Confirm the notice period on our eviction notice page.
  • Collect the lease, the rent ledger and proof of delivery for any demand.
  • Ask the clerk of superior court for the current forms and fees.
  • Speak with a landlord-tenant attorney before filing if the lease is unusual.

When the tenant is willing to leave on a set date, a written move-out agreement can save the filing fee and the wait for a writ. Keep it in plain terms and have an attorney review it.

More questions about North Carolina Eviction Process (Summary Ejectment) and Selling a Rented House

What is summary ejectment in North Carolina?

It is the court action a landlord files to recover possession of rental property. The clerk issues a summons and a magistrate hears the case in small claims court, based on grounds in G.S. 42-26.

How fast is a North Carolina eviction hearing?

The summons sets a date no more than seven days after issuance, and the Judicial Branch says eviction hearings are usually held within 10 to 15 days of filing. Small claims dates are set within 30 days at the outside.

How long does a tenant have to appeal?

Ten days after the magistrate's decision, orally in court or in writing. Appeal costs must be paid and a bond may be required to stop enforcement.

Does a tenant get a jury trial in an eviction case?

No. The Judicial Branch states there is no jury trial in small claims.

Can the landlord keep the tenant's belongings after the writ?

Not at first. Within seven days of taking lawful possession the landlord must release property on request. After that, if the tenant did not retrieve it, G.S. 42-25.9(g) governs disposal.

title: North Carolina Closing Costs for Sellers: Excise Tax, Attorney and Recording

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a North Carolina Closing Costs for Sellers sale

Selling a North Carolina House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Preparing deeds and passing on title is the practice of law, requiring an NC licensed attorney. (N.C.G.S. 84-2.1(a); source)
Selling in North Carolina?
We buy North Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Typical total seller cost figures.

North Carolina closing costs FAQ

Who pays the North Carolina excise tax?

The seller pays it to the register of deeds before recording.

What closing costs does a North Carolina seller actually pay?

A North Carolina seller pays the deed excise tax, the cost of paying off any existing loan, a closing attorney, and the recording charge for any paper the seller must file. The exact total depends on the contract, so the settlement statement from the closing attorney is the document to check line by line.

Some charges are fixed by statute and some are negotiated in the sales contract. This page sticks to the ones the General Statutes spell out, because those do not change from one closing table to the next.

  • The excise tax on the deed, which the law puts on the seller.
  • The payoff of the mortgage or deed of trust, plus the work needed to get that lien cleared from the record.
  • Attorney fees for the person who handles the deed and the title review.
  • Recording fees at the register of deeds for any document the seller has to file.
  • The county property tax bill for the year, which has its own due date and interest schedule.

Commission, repair credits and similar items come from the contract, not the statutes. Ask the listing agent or closing attorney to put every one of them in writing before you sign.

Why does a North Carolina home sale need an attorney?

Under G.S. 84-2.1, drafting a deed or passing upon a title is legal work, so a lawyer has to do it. The definition names deeds, mortgages and title abstracting by name.

The same statute lets a real estate broker fill in a preprinted form, and it lets any person or website complete a preprinted residential lease. It then adds that nobody without a law license may prepare a contract or deed that conveys an interest in North Carolina real property for a third person. That is why closings here are run out of law offices.

Choose, or at least approve, the closing lawyer early. That person reviews the title history, gathers the payoff number, drafts the deed and sees that the deed tax and filing charge reach the county. When a cash buyer names the lawyer, you can still request the draft settlement statement ahead of the closing date.

How does the excise tax fit into a seller's closing costs?

The seller owes it. G.S. 105-228.30 prices a conveyance at one dollar per $500 block of price or value, partial blocks included, and puts the payment on the transferor ahead of filing.

Since the charge follows the price, it is often the biggest line the statutes hand a seller. The lawyer normally subtracts it from your proceeds and delivers it with the deed. A parcel spread over two counties is taxed in whichever one holds more of its value.

Our excise tax page covers the exempt transfers and where the money is routed.

Which recording fees does the register of deeds charge?

Filing charges come from G.S. 161-10, one schedule for all counties. They are collected up front, and the statute calls the list complete and exclusive.

Document or serviceFee as the statute prints it
Ordinary instrument, pages 1 through 15$26.00, then $4.00 per extra page
Mortgage or deed of trust, pages 1 through 35$64.00, then $4.00 per extra page
Satisfaction or cancellation of a loan lienNo fee
Plat$21.00 per sheet
Certified copy$5.00 first page, $2.00 each added page
Nonstandard document$25.00 added charge
Extra instruments inside one document$10.00 each

Source: G.S. 161-10, North Carolina General Assembly. A seller's deed falls in the first row. The mortgage row belongs to the buyer's lender and rarely shows on the seller's side.

What happens to my mortgage payoff and the recorded lien?

After your loan is paid in full, the lender has 30 days to submit a release of the lien. G.S. 45-36.9 sets that clock, and the filing carries no fee.

A late lender owes you actual damages. You may also send a written demand by a method that proves receipt. If another 30 days pass after the lender gets it, the statute adds $1,000 plus reasonable lawyer fees and court costs. Only the landowner who sent the demand holds that right, and it cannot be assigned.

A credit line or future-advance loan needs one more step: the creditor must also receive a request to close the line. Have the attorney send that request with the payoff letter so the lien does not linger on the record.

When does a deed take effect against other buyers and lenders?

Until a deed is registered where the land sits, the buyer has no protection against lien creditors or other purchasers. G.S. 47-18 applies the same rule to contracts to convey, options, leases over three years, and rights of first refusal or first offer.

Priority runs by time of registration. Attorneys therefore file on the day funds move, with the deed tax paid first. As a seller, hold the recording confirmation before you treat the sale as finished.

  • Ask when the deed will be recorded and by whom.
  • Ask for the book and page or document number once it posts.
  • Keep the recorded satisfaction of your old loan with your closing papers.

How do property taxes show up at a North Carolina closing?

A county bill falls due September 1 of its fiscal year and costs face value if paid before January 6. After that, G.S. 105-360 adds two percent interest, then three-fourths of one percent for every month from February 1.

The lien arrives before the bill does. G.S. 105-355 attaches it to the parcel on the listing date under G.S. 105-285, penalties and interest included, so a title search checks tax status early.

The contract decides who bears what share of the year's bill. Request the bill and payment status from the county tax office, and have the attorney explain the division before you count on a net figure.

What should I ask my closing attorney before signing?

Request a written list of every deduction from your proceeds, with its source. One conversation before closing day catches most surprises.

  • What price is the deed tax figured on, and which county takes it?
  • What is the payoff figure, and who tracks the lender's release?
  • Which filing charges are mine and which are the buyer's?
  • How does the contract divide the property tax bill?
  • When will the deed be filed, and will you send the confirmation?

Run the same list on every offer you compare. The statutory items stay put whatever the buyer, so differences come from contract terms.

Do closing costs change if the house is in foreclosure?

Yes, because a power-of-sale foreclosure puts the timing in the hands of the clerk of superior court and the upset bid process. Under G.S. 45-21.27, a higher bid must top the reported price or last bid by at least 5 percent, with a minimum increase of $750, and it carries a deposit of at least 5 percent of that bid, never under $750. Each new bid restarts a ten-day window.

An owner who sells before the sale concludes avoids that uncertainty, but the payoff figure may include costs the lender added. Ask for an itemized payoff in writing and give it to the closing attorney on the first day.

More questions about North Carolina Closing Costs for Sellers

Who bears the deed tax on a North Carolina sale?

The seller. G.S. 105-228.30 puts the payment on the transferor, normally deducted from proceeds by the closing lawyer.

Can I close without a lawyer in North Carolina?

Not in practice. G.S. 84-2.1 counts deed drafting and title review as practicing law, and only a broker's preprinted form or a lease form is carved out.

What does filing my loan release cost?

Nothing. G.S. 161-10 lists no charge for a satisfaction, and the lender has 30 days after payoff to submit it under G.S. 45-36.9.

What does the county charge to file a standard deed?

$26.00 covers pages 1 through 15 and each extra page adds $4.00 under G.S. 161-10. Ask the office about a nonstandard-document add-on.

Where is the deed tax paid for land in two counties?

In the county holding the larger share of the land's value, per G.S. 105-228.30. Have the attorney confirm which office takes the deed.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

North Carolina probate runs through the elected register of deeds.

What the official sources say

  • The elected Clerk of Superior Court acts as probate judge. (NC Judicial Branch: Estates; source)
  • Letters testamentary or of administration are issued by the clerk; filing fee quoted as $120. (NC Judicial Branch: Estates; source)
  • Land and houses generally are not administered through the probate estate unless the will provides or sale is needed to pay debts. (NC Judicial Branch: Estates; source)
  • Collection by affidavit: intestate estate personal property up to $20,000 (up to $30,000 for surviving spouse sole heir), after 30 days. (N.C.G.S. 28A-25-1(a); source)
  • Summary administration is available when the surviving spouse is sole heir or devisee. (NC Judicial Branch: Estates; source)
  • G.S. 105-32.2 (estate tax) repealed effective January 1, 2013, applicable to decedents dying on or after that date. (N.C.G.S. 105-32.2; source)

What we could not confirm

  • Small estate affidavit steps for real property.

North Carolina probate FAQ

Who handles probate in North Carolina?

The register of deeds acts as probate judge.

Who handles probate in North Carolina?

The elected clerk of superior court in each county serves as the probate judge. Clerks and their assistant clerks hear most estate matters, and a judge of the superior court only steps in when someone challenges a will in a caveat proceeding.

The register of deeds is a different office. It records deeds and collects the excise tax, but it does not open estates or issue letters. A family selling a late relative's house will meet both offices, the clerk early and the register at the end.

Is a house part of the North Carolina probate estate?

Not always. The Judicial Branch explains that land and houses are generally not administered through the probate estate unless the will says otherwise or the house must be sold to pay the estate's debts.

State law still decides who holds title. Under G.S. 28A-15-2, title to a decedent's real property vests in the heirs at the moment of death, and property left by a valid probated will vests in the devisees, with that ownership relating back to the date of death. A personal representative can ask the clerk by petition to sell the real property to pay debts and other claims (G.S. 28A-17-1).

With no will, intestacy law names the heirs. A spouse and children share in many cases, a spouse and parents share when there are no children, and a decedent with children but no spouse passes property to the children and the descendants of any child who has died. If no spouse, child or descendant survives, assets generally pass in this order: parents, then siblings and their descendants, then grandparents, then aunts, uncles and their descendants. Property held with a right of survivorship or with a living named beneficiary, such as life insurance, retirement accounts, joint bank accounts and annuities, moves outside the estate. Because the rules differ by situation, ask the clerk of superior court in the decedent's county whether an estate should be opened before you sign a listing agreement.

What are the main probate routes for a North Carolina estate?

Source: NC Judicial Branch estates page and G.S. 28A-25-1
RouteWhen it fitsKey detail
Full administrationEstates that need a court-appointed representativeClerk issues letters; filing fee quoted at $120
Summary administrationSurviving spouse is the sole heir or deviseeAvailable with or without a will
Collection by affidavitSmall estates of personal propertyUp to $20,000, or up to $30,000 for a sole-heir spouse, after 30 days

The courts also run an online guide-and-file service for year's allowance, summary administration and small estate administration, and the clerk's office can say which forms apply.

How does a North Carolina small estate affidavit work?

An heir, a creditor or a public administrator can collect a decedent's personal property by affidavit at least 30 days after death, if the personal property less liens does not exceed $20,000 and no one has petitioned for or been granted letters. A surviving spouse who is the sole heir may use the process for an estate that, after reducing for the spousal allowance, runs above $20,000 but no higher than $30,000.

The affidavit goes to the clerk of superior court in the county where the decedent lived, and it must describe each tract of real property the decedent owned. The process itself covers personal property such as bank accounts and vehicles. If the estate holds a house, ask the clerk how that tract is to be handled and whether the sale needs a representative with letters.

How do you open a full estate with the North Carolina clerk?

Go to the clerk's office for the decedent's home county. Some clerks take walk-ins, and others want an appointment. Bring the original will if one exists, a certified death certificate, a completed application and preliminary inventory, and the $120 filing fee quoted by the court system.

  • An executor named in the will has top priority to receive letters, followed by any named substitute.
  • Without a will, the order runs from the surviving spouse to anyone receiving property under the will, then anyone who would inherit without one, next of kin, creditors, and finally a person of good character living in the county.
  • Out-of-state executors generally post a bond, and administrators post one unless an exception applies.
  • An estate can be reopened later if newly found property turns up.

A person who lived outside North Carolina can have an estate opened in any North Carolina county where property was left.

How long is the creditor window in a North Carolina estate?

The claims deadline must sit at least three months after the notice is first published or posted. After letters issue, the personal representative must run the notice weekly for four straight weeks in a newspaper qualified to carry legal advertisements, or post it where the statute allows if the county has none.

Known creditors get a copy by personal delivery or first class mail within 75 days after letters are granted, and the state's Division of Health Benefits is notified when the decedent received medical assistance. Ask your title agent how it treats the claims period.

What taxes and costs come up when selling an inherited North Carolina house?

The legislature repealed the state estate tax for deaths from January 1, 2013 forward, so those estates owe none. The recurring costs are property tax and the sale itself.

  • County property tax falls due each September 1, and interest starts accruing January 6.
  • The seller covers the deed excise tax at recording time: a dollar for each $500 of value, rounding any partial $500 up.
  • Recording a standard deed costs $26.00 for its first 15 pages, then $4.00 per added page.

When a representative signs the deed, ask the title company which estate documents it needs to see, and request certified copies of the letters from the clerk in advance.

Which North Carolina office should you call first?

The first call belongs to the decedent's home-county clerk, because that office knows whether a will has been filed and whether an estate is already open. Wills become public records once filed, and anyone may view one or request a copy for a fee. North Carolina law does not require a formal reading of a will, so families can move straight to filing it with the clerk and applying for letters.

If no will turns up, the court system suggests contacting clerks in other counties where the person once lived, since some people deposit a will for safekeeping with a clerk. After that, contact the register of deeds where the house stands to find out how the deed is currently titled.

More questions about North Carolina Probate Process and Small Estate Affidavit for Real Estate

Who is the probate judge in North Carolina?

The elected clerk of superior court in each county acts as the probate judge. A superior court judge hears a caveat proceeding when a will's validity is challenged.

What is the North Carolina small estate affidavit limit?

It is $20,000 in personal property after liens for most estates. A surviving spouse who is the sole heir may use it up to $30,000, after any spousal allowance is subtracted.

What is the filing fee to open a North Carolina estate?

The court system quotes a $120 filing fee. Bring the will, a certified death certificate and the application and inventory forms. Forms are available from the clerk's office and on the court system's website, and the court system offers an online guide-and-file tool for simpler estates.

Does North Carolina have an estate tax?

No. The estate tax statutes were repealed effective January 1, 2013, for deaths from that date on.

Is a house sale possible while a North Carolina estate is open?

Possibly, but who can sign depends on the will and on the heirs. Title to real property vests in the heirs or devisees at death, and a representative can petition the clerk to sell for debts, so confirm the route with the clerk of superior court first.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a North Carolina Excise Tax on Deeds sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

North Carolina charges an excise tax on conveyances of real property.

What the official sources say

  • Half of proceeds go to the county general fund; half goes to the State (less county allowance). (N.C.G.S. 105-228.30(b); source)
  • Exempt transfers include by operation of law, lease, will, intestacy, gift, no consideration, merger, and instruments securing debt. (N.C.G.S. 105-228.29; source)
Selling in North Carolina?
We buy North Carolina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • County level exceptions.

North Carolina excise tax FAQ

What is the North Carolina excise tax rate?

The statute cited above sets it at $1 per $500 of consideration.

What is the North Carolina excise tax on deeds?

It is a levy on each document that conveys an interest in North Carolina real estate. G.S. 105-228.30 sets it at a single dollar for every block of five hundred dollars in the consideration or value of what changes hands.

The statute rounds up. Each time the price crosses into a new block of five hundred, the charge steps up by another dollar, even if the new block is barely begun. For an ordinary sale the base is the price written in the contract.

Every county applies the same rate, since the rule is statewide. Only the office you visit changes with the location of the land.

Who pays the excise tax, the buyer or the seller?

The seller does. The law calls the seller the transferor and makes that person responsible for paying the county recording office ahead of recording.

At a typical closing the attorney holds back the amount from sale proceeds and sends it along with the deed. A cash buyer or investor changes nothing here. A contract may ask the buyer to cover a closing item, but that is a bargain between the two parties, and the statute still names the transferor.

  • The timing is fixed: payment precedes recording.
  • The recipient is the office in the county where the land lies.
  • The charge follows the deed, whoever ends up as the buyer.

Our closing costs page shows where this tax sits among the other seller charges.

Where does the excise tax money go?

The proceeds are shared equally between two recipients. The home county takes one share for its general fund. The second share, less refunds and an allowance, goes to the Department of Revenue every month, and the county may retain two percent of it.

This split explains why you pay locally and not in Raleigh. The county collects first and forwards the state portion later.

A parcel that straddles a county line is assigned to one county only: the one holding the larger share of its value. If your land crosses a line, ask the attorney which recording office will take the deed, because that office decides where the paperwork lands.

Which transfers are exempt from the excise tax?

Eight categories escape the tax under G.S. 105-228.29. A normal home sale fits none of them, since a sale means money or property flowing to the seller.

Transfer typePlace in the statute
By operation of lawSubdivision (1)
Lease for a term of yearsSubdivision (2)
Under a willSubdivision (3)
By intestacySubdivision (4)
By giftSubdivision (5)
No money or property due from the transfereeSubdivision (6)
Merger, conversion or consolidationSubdivision (7)
Instrument securing a debtSubdivision (8)

Source: G.S. 105-228.29, North Carolina General Assembly. Row eight is why a lender's security instrument escapes the tax that a sale deed carries.

How does the excise tax relate to inherited property?

A transfer that happens through a will or through intestacy is exempt, so the heirs owe nothing when title first passes to them.

The charge appears when they sell. A deed from the heirs to a buyer is a transfer for consideration, so the sellers owe it, and with several heirs the attorney pays it out of the combined proceeds.

The state has also dropped its own estate tax for anyone who died from January 1, 2013 onward. Read the repeal notice for Article 1A of Chapter 105 if you want the exact wording. The deed charge discussed here is a different tax and still applies to a sale of inherited land.

Does paying the excise tax also record the deed?

No. Payment is a gate that comes first, and the filing is a separate act with its own charge, which our closing costs page lists from G.S. 161-10.

The filing matters because of G.S. 47-18. Until a conveyance is registered, it gives way to lien creditors and paying purchasers, and priority runs by the sequence of registration.

  • Pay the levy first.
  • Have the deed registered where the land lies.
  • Keep the receipted copy with your sale papers.

Recording a satisfaction of a deed of trust carries no fee, so a mortgage payoff adds no filing charge. A lease longer than three years, an option and a right of first refusal follow the same registration rule, so mention any side agreement to the attorney early.

What should a seller confirm about the excise tax before closing?

Confirm three things: the amount the tax is computed from, the county that receives it, and the settlement statement line that shows it.

  • The contract price and any other value that counts as consideration.
  • The county whose office will take the deed.
  • Whether an exemption in G.S. 105-228.29 really applies, for example a gift where nothing comes back to you.
  • That the tax shows once on the seller side of the statement.

Call the county office to learn how it accepts deeds for recording. The rate is statewide, and the procedure is where counties can differ.

What other tax bills can come due when a North Carolina owner sells?

The county property bill is the main one. Under G.S. 105-277.1B, a senior or permanently disabled homeowner who has lived in the house for years can see the annual bill limited to a share of income, 4.0 percent in the lower band and 5.0 percent in the upper one. Whatever exceeds that share is postponed and sits on the property as a lien.

A sale ends the arrangement, as do the owner's death or a move out of the home. Three fiscal years of postponed tax then come due. A seller who used this relief should request that number from the county tax office well ahead of closing, since it lands next to the deed levy in the seller's column.

The disabled veteran exclusion under G.S. 105-277.1C takes a fixed slice of appraised value, printed in the statute as $45,000, out of the tax base for a qualifying veteran or surviving spouse. Ask the county assessor how a sale affects that exclusion.

Does the deed tax apply to a contract for deed?

The statute taxes each instrument that conveys an interest in real property. A contract for deed under Chapter 47H is a different paper: the seller keeps title while the buyer makes five or more payments, and the contract covers one to four family dwellings priced at $5,000 or more.

Chapter 47H demands a signed, acknowledged writing, lets the buyer back out through the third business day, and requires the seller to file the contract itself or a short memorandum within five business days. Whether and when a deed tax is owed on such a deal depends on the instrument used, so have the attorney confirm the answer before anyone signs.

More questions about North Carolina Excise Tax on Deeds

What rate applies to a North Carolina deed?

One dollar per five hundred dollars of consideration or value, with any leftover fraction counted as a full block. The same rate applies in all counties under G.S. 105-228.30.

Does the buyer cover the deed tax?

By default no. The statute puts the duty on the transferor, though a sales contract may move the cost by agreement between the parties.

Can a gift of a house avoid the tax?

A true gift is exempt under G.S. 105-228.29. If the recipient pays money or gives property in return, the no-consideration exemption fails, so check with the closing attorney before you rely on it.

Which office takes the payment?

The county recording office where the property sits. For land in several counties, the county with the larger share of the value takes it.

Is there a state estate tax on top of the deed tax?

No. The estate tax sections in Chapter 105, Article 1A, were repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2013, and the deed levy is separate.
